newsitem.title: FRANCE: French election depends on turnout, National Front.
newsitem.headline: French election depends on turnout, National Front.

text.p: Voter turnout and the ballots cast by supporters of the far-right National Front are keys to the outcome of Sunday's parliamentary election in France, political analysts said on Friday.
The French left, which scored an upset win in the first round, has the momentum going into Sunday's runoff vote even though a comeback by the governing centre-right cannot be ruled out, they say.

"One has to be very prudent. Things can go either way," said Dominique Moisi of the French Institute for International Relations, predicting a slim victory whichever side wins a National Assembly majority.

"For now the momentum is on the left. But the emergence of Philippe Seguin and Alain Madelin as the new leaders of the centre-right campaign could trigger an opposing trend towards the right," said Gilles Corman of the Sofres polling firm.

Typically in France's two-round election system, voter turnout is lower in the runoff. But in Sunday's poll, analysts are virtually unanimous in predicting a higher turnout, a factor which should boost the right's prospects.
"On the first-round vote, more rightists stayed home than leftists. So if the turnout is higher on the second round, that should help the right," said Corman. Turnout last Sunday was 68 percent.
He acknowledged the boost could be partially offset by a similar phenomenon on the left, in which leftist voters might vote after abstaining on the first round when many saw little chance of victory.

The impact of the runoff choices made by supporters of the xenophobic National Front, whose leader Jean-Marie Le Pen openly embraces racial inequality and has repeatedly insisted that Nazi gas chambers were "a detail of history", is more difficult to pin down, analysts said.

Thanks to its 14.94-percent score in last Sunday's first round, the Front is competing in a record 132 of France's 577 constituencies in the runoff round, including 73 three-way contests in which it faces both a leftist and a rightist.
In France, any candidate winning at least 12.5 percent of a district's registered voters is entitled to stand in a runoff.
In the three-way races, the right is the big loser as the Front candidate splits the rightist vote, favouring leftists.
National Front voters' above-average motivation also works against the right, analysts say.
However, in districts where there is no National Front candidate, first-round Front voters are more likely to turn to a rightist in the runoff, voter surveys have found.

In addition, some Front voters, fearing a leftist victory, may turn to mainstream rightists even in constituencies where there is a Front candidate, who would stand little or no chance of winning a seat in parliament in any case, Corman said.
In a close contest between the left and the right, these patterns could give the mainstream right the votes it needs to hold on to a majority of seats in the National Assembly.
But should the left take a strong overall lead, as trends indicate, that would not be enough to head off a leftist majority, analysts predict.

"The great unknown is how National Front voters will behave. Their decisions in the final days of the campaign will be of equal importance to the abstention rate in determining the final outcome," Corman said.
Another factor difficult to gauge is Gaullist Prime Minister Alain Juppe's decision to step down and the emergence of Seguin and Madelin as the government's de facto campaign leaders.
"It can only be positive" for the right, said Moisi. "Philippe Seguin has a strong, charismatic personality."
